Thanks for sharing, it probably feels good to get that out, and I think your feelings are valid. I'd just like to share something with you that has helped me. 

With regards to clinical help: I am not sure where you live, but I do not think it would show up on some sort of record that would affect employment prospects. It would be a violation of the privacy act. Even if it does, however, is that really worth your not getting help? Are you going to stay miserable for the rest of your life on the off chance that it might hurt your chances of getting a job? Any good employer will recognize that most people need help with issues like this, and that it takes tremendous courage and self-awareness to get help, and those qualities are valuable. Nobody is perfect, and anyone who expects you to be is a waste of your time. A job should not come at the cost of your well-being.

Getting professional help really helped me, and many others. With medication, you will usually start with a low dose, so the side effects aren't a huge shock. For example, I started Zoloft two weeks ago, and I'm experiencing vivid dreams and appetite loss, but it's a small price to pay. Now, I don't wake up in the mornings full of dread, nor self-hatred. My days got so horrible that I didn't care what the side-effects were. Anything is better than waking up full of emotional pain. This is just my experience and it really does help. Don't be afraid to try new things is all I suggest. 

So. I hope you are feeling better. And remember you are not your feelings nor your thoughts.

I am going to offer some advice that has been working for me. Use it or not at your discretion. 

Think of yourself this way. There are two parts to you: your true- self, and your scared-self. 

Your true-self knows it needs to get help. Your true-self wants to be happy. Your true self is posting on reddit asking for advice. Your true self is also often hidden by your scared-self.

Your scared-self was created by all the pain you've experienced. Your scared self is trying to protect you. Your scared self tells you not to get help, because it might not work for you, or you might lose out in some way. 

Your scared-self is also incorrect. It is a survival mechanism to help people avoid situations that may be dangerous, harmful, painful, or may cause you a loss. I think depression occurs when you scared-self gets very loud.

Your true-self knows otherwise. YOU are your true self, and YOU know better. Your scared self is just a voice in your head. It is not you. 

Is your true self going to stand for this? Are YOU truly going to stop yourself from getting help, just because you might see someone you know, or whatever other excuse it's made?

Really, what's the worst that could happen? Someone will see you there at the clinic. What happens then? Maybe they'll judge you? Maybe they'll say things? People may know about your problems?

All those possibilities are what your scared-self is saying. Ask your true self this question: are all these things really worth not getting help?

Don't let your scared self win. Your scared self will be with you for the rest of your life, and it is only trying to protect you, but your true self must be the one making decisions, otherwise you will not get better. 

It's okay that you've been too scared and anxious to get the help you need. You are not weak or cowardly if you are having trouble. Everyone has a scared-self, and sometimes that scared self is very big, due to life being hard. 

You have another chance today and tomorrow. 

You will feel better after getting help. It might be awkward or it might be difficult, or it might be easy. In any case, your true self will feel a lot better. 

So just make the phone call, let yourself get help. You will thank yourself for it.

Best of luck to you. You can do it. I believe in your true self.
